Toward its objective of preparing a comprehensive plan, the Northeastern Illinois Planning Commission, in September, 1964, entered into a contract with the State of Illinois, Department of Public Works and Buildings, Division of Highways, in cooperation with the U.S. Department of Transportation, Federal Highway Administration, Bureau of Public Roads. Under the terms of this contract NIPC agreed to develop several land use alternatives for the six counties with a target year of 1990.5 This was to be the first step in an interagency planning process that was to lead eventually to an optimum comprehensive plan of development (including transportation) for the six-county area. CATS was to estimate the travel demand generated by each land use alternative within their study area as described above. By estimating how future trips would be made on CATS proposed network of expressway and transit facilities, it would be possible to compare the effectiveness of the several alternative patterns of land use in reducing the time and cost of travel. At a later stage, when the choice among land use alternatives had been narrowed, it would be possible to test the relative efficiency of two or more transportation networks against a given land use pattern.
On April 19, 1968, the Northeastern Illinois Planning Commission adopted the plan entitled "The Comprehensive General Plan for the Development of the Northeastern Illinois Counties Area."
Within the six county Illinois portion of the region there have been four major transportation studies: Fox River Valley Transportation Study; Joliet Area Transportation Study; Lake County Transportation Study; and the Chicago Area Transportation Study (CATS). Only a few years ago planning for the future system came under the aegis of a single transportation agency (CATS).
In March 1971, the Chicago Area Transportation Study produced the document entitled Regional Transportation Interim Plan and Program. On October 21, 1971, the Northeastern Illinois Planning Commission adopted the Interim Transportation Plan and Program as one of its functional plans. Lincoln Highway was shown as an arterial in the plan.
